title: The Gold Standard: When Money Meant Something
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the gold standard: how a currency is redeemable for gold, why gold was chosen, the US bimetallic period and the 15-to-1 and 16-to-1 silver ratios, the Civil War greenbacks and the Long Depression, the 1900 Gold Standard Act, the classic gold standard era and its end at World War One, the 1930s bank runs and the UK's 1931 exit, FDR's banking holiday and the 1934 Gold Reserve Act, Bretton Woods and Nixon's 1971 suspension, and the modern debate between gold bugs and fiat-currency supporters, including inflation, money supply, national debt, cryptocurrency, and a gold-versus-stock-market comparison. Ends with a listener mail about classroom questioning.
topics: Isaac Newton Master of the Mint

segments.title: Opening banter and gold standard basics
segments.summary: Hosts joke about never having seen gold and introduce the gold standard, in which paper money is redeemable for gold and money supply is limited by gold reserves.

segments.title: Benefits of gold standard and gold bugs
segments.summary: Stability of prices and trade effects of a gold standard are described, and the term gold bugs is introduced, referencing Edgar Allan Poe.

segments.title: Why gold, and the bimetallic silver ratio
segments.summary: Gold was chosen for scarcity, divisibility and durability. The US set a silver-to-gold ratio of fifteen to one, later changed to sixteen to one.

segments.title: Gold and silver imbalances and gold rushes
segments.summary: Fixed ratios are artificial, so gold and silver values shift; people hoard or melt coins, and gold rushes in California and Australia pushed the government to give up on bimetallism.

segments.title: Britain adopts gold standard
segments.summary: Isaac Newton as Master of the Mint favored gold, and Britain adopted the gold standard around 1819, with the idea spreading through Europe.

segments.title: Civil War currency chaos and greenbacks
segments.summary: Before the war there were thousands of local currencies. The Civil War led to war bonds and unbacked paper currency, causing about 25 percent inflation.

segments.title: Lincoln's currency destruction and the Long Depression
segments.summary: Rising national debt and inflation prompted the government to withdraw and destroy bills, which deflated the economy and triggered the Long Depression from 1873 to 1879.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the next section.

segments.title: Classic gold standard era and the 1900 Gold Standard Act
segments.summary: Global globalization in the 1870s led to a golden age of the gold standard until World War One. The Greenback and silver movements lost, and the Gold Standard Act of 1900 tied currency to gold. Stability in trade and shipping is described.

segments.title: World War One ends the classic gold standard
segments.summary: Wartime spending and gold constraints led Europe to abandon the international gold standard, while the US and UK kept it. The dollar and pound became reserve currencies.

segments.title: 1930s bank runs and UK exit from gold
segments.summary: The 1929 crash and bank runs closed about ten thousand US banks before FDIC. The UK abandoned gold in 1931, with the story of Montagu Norman's breakdown; Hoover handed the crisis to FDR.

segments.title: FDR's banking holiday and gold confiscation
segments.summary: FDR declared a four-day banking holiday and the Emergency Banking Act followed. Hoarders were threatened with penalties for keeping gold.

segments.title: Ending the US gold standard and its role in recovery
segments.summary: The US suspended the gold standard and the Gold Reserve Act of 1934 banned private gold bars. Economists say leaving gold let the US print money to exit the Great Depression.

segments.title: Break and listener mail teaser
segments.summary: Ad break; hosts tease that the gold standard had a later revival.

segments.title: Bretton Woods and Nixon's 1971 end
segments.summary: The Bretton Woods Agreement of 1944 pegged the US dollar to gold at thirty-five dollars an ounce. Growing spending meant the US lacked gold, and Nixon ended convertibility in 1971.

segments.title: Gold standard end and modern gold bugs
segments.summary: The IMF moved off gold in 1973, and gold standard advocacy became a fringe position. Milton Friedman opposed returning to gold.

segments.title: Arguments for and against gold; inflation and money supply
segments.summary: Pro-gold arguments cite limits on spending and stability; anti-gold arguments cite flexibility and fiat tools. The hosts cite purchasing power declines, M2 money supply growth and national debt growth since 1970.

segments.title: Gold total value versus global economy; bitcoin comparison
segments.summary: Total gold value is about thirty-six trillion dollars against a global economy near one hundred twenty-six trillion, so a gold standard could not cover it. Bitcoin's fixed supply is compared to gold as a deflationary asset.

segments.title: Gold versus stock market returns
segments.summary: A hypothetical five thousand dollar investment in 1971 gold versus the S&P 500 is compared, with the stock market producing far larger returns, adjusted for inflation too.

segments.title: Credits and research notes
segments.summary: Hosts credit the research and acknowledge simplifications in the monetary policy discussion.

segments.title: Listener mail: classroom question hack
segments.summary: A middle school teacher named Aaron from New Brunswick, Canada suggests asking What questions do you have? instead of Does anyone have any questions? to encourage students.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and the show's contact and credit lines.
